source.author: lucan
source.text: Non Taenareis sic faucibus aer Sedit iners, moestum mundi confine latentis, Ac nostri: quo non metuant emittere manes Tartarei reges, Nam quamvis Thessala vates Vim faciat fatis, dubium est, quod traxerit illuc Aspiciat Stygias, an quod descenderit, umbras.
source.text_original: Non Taenareis sic faucibus aer / Sedit iners, moestum mundi confine latentis, / Ac nostri: quo non metuant emittere manes / Tartarei reges, Nam quamvis Thessala vates / Vim faciat fatis, dubium est, quod traxerit illuc / Aspiciat Stygias, an quod descenderit, umbras.
source.text_english: Not so in the Taenarian jaws did the air sit idle, the sorrowful borderland of the hidden world, as of ours: where the kings of Tartarus fear not to let the shades escape, for although the Thessalian prophetess may exert force over the fates, it is doubtful whether she drew the Stygian shades there to look upon them, or whether she descended to them.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: securus in aequor haut minus Erginus, proles Neptunia, fertur, qui maris insidias, clarae qui sidera noctis norit et e clausis quem destinet Aeolus antris, non metuat cui regna ratis, cui tradere caelum assidua Tiphys vultum lassatus ab Arcto.
reuse.text_original: securus in aequor / haut minus Erginus, proles Neptunia, fertur, / qui maris insidias, clarae qui sidera noctis / norit et e clausis quem destinet Aeolus antris, / non metuat cui regna ratis, cui tradere caelum / assidua Tiphys vultum lassatus ab Arcto.
reuse.text_english: Secure, into the sea is borne Erginus, no less so, a child of Neptune, one who knows the sea’s ambushes, one who knows the stars of the clear night and whom Aeolus dispatches from his closed caves, who need not fear the ship’s dominion, to whom Tiphys, worn out by constant watch, wishes to entrust the sky, steering from the North.
